---
title: "Choosing a mixture with BIC"
execute:
  cache: false
---

A Gaussian mixture requires both a component count and a covariance family. We use the [**Bayesian information criterion (BIC)**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) to compare a declared grid on the [speaker-relative Peterson-Barney representation](distance-and-scaling.qmd), then distinguish the selected distributional model from the ten-component model used to teach membership and external alignment.

## Reconstructing the candidate data

```{r}
source_environment <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
utils::data("pb52", package = "phonTools", envir = source_environment)
pb52 <- source_environment$pb52
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(mclust))

stopifnot(
  identical(dim(pb52), c(1520L, 9L)),
  length(unique(pb52$speaker)) == 76L,
  all(table(pb52$speaker) == 20L)
)

vowels <- pb52 |>
  dplyr::group_by(speaker) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    z_f1 = (f1 - mean(f1)) / stats::sd(f1),
    z_f2 = (f2 - mean(f2)) / stats::sd(f2)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

X <- as.matrix(vowels[, c("z_f1", "z_f2")])
candidate_models <- c("EEI", "EVI", "VEV", "VVI")
candidate_components <- 2:16
```

For \(p=2\), write
\(\boldsymbol\Sigma_k=\lambda_k\mathbf D_k\mathbf A_k\mathbf D_k^{\mathsf T}\),
where \(\lambda_k\) is volume, \(\mathbf A_k\) is a determinant-one shape,
and \(\mathbf D_k\) is orientation.

| Family | Volume | Shape | Orientation | Covariance parameters in two dimensions |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| `EEI` | equal | equal | coordinate axes | \(2\) |
| `EVI` | equal | varying | coordinate axes | \(1+K\) |
| `VEV` | varying | equal | varying | \(2K+1\) |
| `VVI` | varying | varying | coordinate axes | \(2K\) |

Thus `EEI`, `EVI`, and `VVI` use diagonal covariances, while `VEV` permits rotated
ellipses. The 2--16 grid brackets the ten-category teaching fit and permits
some categories to occupy more than one region without making the candidate
search unbounded. These four families expose contrasts in volume, shape, and
orientation while keeping the grid small enough to inspect. Excluding other
`mclust` families is a teaching-design choice, not evidence that those families
are implausible.

The covariance families and component range are fixed before intended-vowel agreement is inspected. A candidate specification contains the component count $K$, covariance family $\mathcal C$, and remaining procedure $\mathcal R$:

$$
M=\langle K,\mathcal C,\mathcal R\rangle.
$$

Changing the scaling or start policy during the comparison would change $\mathcal R$ and thus the candidate being ranked.

## BIC and its sign convention

For maximized likelihood $L$, $q$ estimated parameters, and $n$ likelihood contributions, define

$$
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\log L+q\log n.
$$

Smaller values are preferred under this convention. `mclust` reports the negative quantity,

$$
\operatorname{BIC}_{\texttt{mclust}}
=
2\log L-q\log n,
$$

so its larger value is better. We convert the sign before plotting.

## Fitting the declared grid

```{r}
set.seed(1952L)
bic_object <- mclust::mclustBIC(
  X,
  G = candidate_components,
  modelNames = candidate_models,
  verbose = FALSE
)

bic_grid <- as.data.frame(as.table(as.matrix(bic_object))) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    components = as.integer(as.character(Var1)),
    covariance_model = as.character(Var2),
    mclust_bic_larger_is_better = as.numeric(Freq),
    conventional_bic_smaller_is_better =
      -mclust_bic_larger_is_better
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(is.finite(mclust_bic_larger_is_better))

best_bic <- bic_grid |>
  dplyr::slice_min(
    conventional_bic_smaller_is_better,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

set.seed(1952L)
fit_g14 <- mclust::Mclust(
  X,
  G = best_bic$components,
  modelNames = best_bic$covariance_model,
  verbose = FALSE
)
set.seed(1952L)
fit_g10 <- mclust::Mclust(
  X,
  G = 10L,
  modelNames = "EVI",
  verbose = FALSE
)

direct_bic_g14 <- -2 * fit_g14$loglik + fit_g14$df * log(nrow(X))
direct_bic_g10 <- -2 * fit_g10$loglik + fit_g10$df * log(nrow(X))

stopifnot(
  best_bic$components == 14L,
  best_bic$covariance_model == "EEI",
  abs(direct_bic_g14 + fit_g14$bic) < 1e-7,
  abs(direct_bic_g10 + fit_g10$bic) < 1e-7
)

fit_comparison <- data.frame(
  candidate = c("14-component EEI", "10-component EVI"),
  log_likelihood = c(fit_g14$loglik, fit_g10$loglik),
  parameters = c(fit_g14$df, fit_g10$df),
  conventional_bic = c(direct_bic_g14, direct_bic_g10)
)
knitr::kable(fit_comparison, digits = 3)
```

The grid selects the `r best_bic$components`-component `r best_bic$covariance_model` model with BIC `r round(best_bic$conventional_bic_smaller_is_better, 3)`. The fixed ten-component `EVI` model has BIC `r round(direct_bic_g10, 3)`. These values are obtained from the fitted likelihoods, parameter counts, and observed token count shown in the table.

The parameter counts can also be reconstructed. Every model has \(K-1\) free
weights and \(2K\) mean coordinates. In two dimensions, the covariance counts in
the table give

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
q_{\mathrm{EEI}}=(K-1)+2K+2=3K+1, &
q_{\mathrm{EVI}}=(K-1)+2K+(K+1)=4K,\\
q_{\mathrm{VEV}}=(K-1)+2K+(2K+1)=5K, &
q_{\mathrm{VVI}}=(K-1)+2K+2K=5K-1.
\end{array}
$$

For the selected row, \(K=`r fit_g14$G`\),
\(\log L=`r round(fit_g14$loglik, 3)`\),
\(q=`r fit_g14$df`\), and \(n=`r nrow(X)`\). Substitution gives

$$
-2(`r round(fit_g14$loglik, 3)`)
+`r fit_g14$df`\log(`r nrow(X)`)
=
`r round(direct_bic_g14, 3)`,
$$

which is the corresponding conventional BIC in the output table.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-alt: "Conventional smaller-is-better BIC across two through sixteen Gaussian mixture components for four declared covariance families."

ggplot2::ggplot(bic_grid, ggplot2::aes(
  x = components,
  y = conventional_bic_smaller_is_better,
  group = covariance_model,
  color = covariance_model
)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.65) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.25) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 16, by = 2)) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.82) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Number of mixture components",
    y = "BIC (smaller is better)",
    color = "Covariance family"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Distributional fit and label alignment differ

```{r}
external_alignment <- data.frame(
  candidate = c("14-component EEI", "10-component EVI"),
  adjusted_rand_index = c(
    mclust::adjustedRandIndex(fit_g14$classification, vowels$vowel),
    mclust::adjustedRandIndex(fit_g10$classification, vowels$vowel)
  )
)
knitr::kable(external_alignment, digits = 3)
```

The BIC-selected model has post-fit ARI `r round(external_alignment$adjusted_rand_index[external_alignment$candidate == "14-component EEI"], 3)`, while the ten-component `EVI` model has ARI `r round(external_alignment$adjusted_rand_index[external_alignment$candidate == "10-component EVI"], 3)`. BIC prefers the first density specification; the external intended-vowel partition aligns more closely with the second hard classification.

This K10/G14 distinction should remain explicit. A particular mixture can be useful for teaching category-aligned uncertainty without being the BIC-selected density model.

## Interpreting the sample size

The criterion uses $n=`r nrow(X)`$ token contributions because that is the likelihood fitted by the software. It does not imply that the study sampled that many independent speakers. The rows come from `r dplyr::n_distinct(vowels$speaker)` speakers with repeated productions.

The usual BIC approximation presumes an appropriate independence structure. A token-level mixture that omits repeated-speaker dependence does not gain that structure from the penalty. Thus, the values can rank these declared software fits, while their asymptotic evidence interpretation remains limited.

## Candidate-set and fit limits

BIC compares only the supplied component counts, covariance families, representation, and fitting controls. It cannot repair omitted F3 information, within-speaker dependence, or an unsuitable Gaussian family. Mixture label permutations and weakly represented components also complicate the regularity assumptions behind simple information-criterion arguments.

There is a deeper approximation limit. The usual BIC derivation uses a regular
Laplace approximation around an interior, locally identifiable maximum. Finite
mixtures can violate these conditions because labels can be permuted, a component
weight can approach zero, and a covariance can approach singularity. BIC remains
a declared ranking rule for these fitted candidates, but its difference should
not be read as exact log model evidence.

The selected component count need not equal a phonological inventory. A vowel's productions may occupy several Gaussian regions, while overlapping intended vowels may share one region.

## Checking the BIC comparison

1. How is each displayed BIC reconstructed from log likelihood and parameter count?
2. Why is the `mclust` sign reversed before plotting?
3. Which declared model minimizes conventional BIC?
4. Which fixed model aligns more closely with intended-vowel metadata?
5. Why does the token count not represent independent speakers?
6. What does the selected component count leave unresolved linguistically?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Insert each fit's `loglik`, `df`, and `r format(nrow(vowels), big.mark = ",")` token contributions into the displayed
   formula.
2. `mclust` reports \(2\log L-q\log n\), the negative of the convention used here.
3. The fourteen-component `EEI` fit minimizes conventional BIC in this grid.
4. The ten-component `EVI` hard classification has higher post-fit ARI.
5. Twenty rows come from each speaker, so token contributions are not independent
   sampled speakers.
6. A selected density component count does not identify a phonological inventory.

</details>

## Recap

1. A candidate includes component count, covariance family, and fitting procedure.
2. BIC combines maximized token likelihood with an explicitly reconstructed
   parameter-count penalty.
3. Mixture singularities and repeated-speaker dependence limit the usual evidence
   approximation.

The [next page](validating-a-mixture.qmd#held-out-log-loss) compares the fixed K10
and G14 candidates by predictive density on complete held-out speakers.
